en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity within the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
2. The Question on Restraint of the Belly “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘One should rise up; one should not be negligent.’”
"One should be restrained regarding the stomach.
Yet, the Blessed One has also said:
"But sometimes, Udāyin, I eat from this bowl until it is level with the rim, and even more than that."
"Venerable Nāgasena, if it was spoken by the Blessed One:

'One should rise up and not be negligent; one should be restrained in eating,' then that statement—'But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat from this bowl until it is level with the rim, and even more than that'—must be false.
If it was indeed spoken by the Tathāgata—"

“But, Udāyin, at times I eat even as much as fills this bowl, and I eat even more than that. In that case, the statement, “One should rise up and not be negligent; one should be restrained in regard to the stomach,” would be false.
This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:”
"‘One should rise up and not be negligent; one should be restrained in eating’—and yet it was said:
‘Indeed, Udāyin, sometimes I eat from this bowl until it is level with the rim, and even more than that.
What has been spoken by the Blessed One, O Great King—"

‘One should rise up; one should not be negligent; one should be restrained in eating’—this is a statement of the true nature, a statement that leaves nothing out, a statement that is exhaustive, a statement that is non-figurative, a statement of what has come to be, a statement that is factual, a statement that is such as it is, a statement that is non-perverted, the word of the seers, the word of the sages, the word of the Blessed One, the word of the Worthy One, the word of the Paccekabuddhas, the word of the Conqueror, the word of the Omniscient One.
This is the word of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
"One who is unrestrained in the belly, Great King, kills living beings, takes what is not given,
commits adultery, speaks falsehood, drinks intoxicants, and even deprives his mother of life and his father of life."
One deprives even an Arahant of life, one causes a schism in the Saṅgha, and with a malicious mind, one sheds the blood of a Tathāgata.
Indeed, Great King, Devadatta, being unrestrained in his belly, incurred an action that lasts for an eon after he had split the Saṅgha.
Having seen many such various reasons as these, Great King, it was said by the Blessed One:
‘One should rise up; one should not be negligent; one should be restrained in the stomach.

Being restrained in the stomach, Great King, one realizes the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, one actualizes the four fruits of asceticism, one attains mastery over the four analytical knowledges, the eight meditative attainments, and the six direct knowledges, and the whole...
He fulfills the duty of a recluse.

Indeed, Great King, did not the young white pigeon, by being self-restrained even within his own belly, cause the realm of the Thirty-three to tremble and lead Sakka, the lord of the devas, to his attendance?
Great King, there are many other such diverse reasons as well.
Having seen this, the Blessed One said:
“One should rise up and not be negligent; one should be restrained in eating.
Furthermore, Great King, that which was spoken by the Blessed One—
‘Indeed, Udāyin, there were times when I ate from this very bowl even until it was level with my mouth, and I ate even more than that’— this was said by the Tathāgata,
the one who has done what was to be done, who has accomplished his task, whose goal is achieved, who has lived the holy life to its conclusion,
who is free from obscurations, the omniscient, the self-become, and the self-awakened one, speaking of himself.
Just as, great king, a sick person who has vomited, purged, and undergone a purgative requires treatment that is suitable to his condition,
even so, great king, one who still possesses defilements and has not yet seen the Truths must practice restraint over the belly.
Just as, great king, for a jewel that is radiant, of noble birth, and perfectly pure, there is no need for further washing, rubbing, or polishing;
“In the same way, Great King, for the Tathāgata who has reached perfection in the domain of a Buddha, there is no obstruction regarding what is to be done or not done.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
The second dilemma: On Self-Restraint of the Belly.
